outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: The Dispute in Context — Financed Auto Policies, Cancellation, and the Road to Appeal
outline.description: This chapter introduces the parties, the premium-finance arrangement that made APAC central to the cancellations, and the events that produced the litigation. It also explains the procedural posture, including the class-action allegations, removal to federal court, the limited summary-judgment issue presented, and the specific errors the plaintiffs asserted on appeal.
subtopics: Who the parties are: Williams, Wright, Jenkins, GoAuto, and APAC
How premium financing worked: APAC paid the full premium and insureds repaid in installments
The power-of-attorney clauses allowing APAC to cancel for uncured nonpayment
Why cancellation mattered in this case, including Jenkins's accident-related stake
The plaintiffs' theories: ineffective cancellation, misrepresentation, and breach of good faith and fair dealing
Removal from Louisiana state court to the Middle District of Louisiana
The parties' cross-motions for summary judgment limited to statutory compliance
The district court's ruling for GoAuto and dismissal of all claims with prejudice
The three appellate arguments: delivery of notice, GoAuto's receipt of cancellation requests, and denial of plaintiffs' partial summary judgment motion

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: The Governing Louisiana Statute — How a Premium Finance Company Cancels an Insurance Policy
outline.description: This chapter sets out the statutory framework the Fifth Circuit had to apply. It explains the required steps under Louisiana Revised Statutes section 9:3550(G), the information that must accompany a cancellation request, and the Louisiana case law insisting on strict adherence. It also shows why the statutory scheme focuses on certainty of cancellation date and a minimum opportunity to cure default.
subtopics: The role of Louisiana Revised Statutes section 9:3550 in financed-policy cancellations
The finance company's authority to act through a valid power of attorney
The insured's default and the prerequisite notice-and-cure period
Section 9:3550(G)(3)(a): the notice of cancellation and the accompanying statement 'certifying' four statutory facts
What the certification must cover: valid power of attorney, uncured default, prior notice to the insured, and notice to other interested persons
Section 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i): the insurer's ability to cancel upon 'receipt' of the notice and statement
Louisiana cases requiring strict adherence to statutory cancellation procedures
The consequences of defect: ineffective cancellation
The two policy functions identified by Louisiana courts: fixing the exact time of cancellation and preserving a minimum cure period

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: GoAuto and APAC's Cancellation Process — The 'Certifying' Question and Whether a Signature Is Required
outline.description: This chapter explains the actual cancellation workflow used by APAC and GoAuto and then analyzes the plaintiffs' first major statutory argument: that APAC's notice was ineffective because it was not signed before GoAuto's system automatically cancelled the policy. The chapter traces how the Fifth Circuit read the word 'certifying,' evaluated the sparse Louisiana authority, distinguished the one case mentioning signatures, and concluded that strict adherence does not permit courts to add a signature requirement not found in the statute.
subtopics: Step-by-step description of the cancellation process used by APAC and GoAuto
The ten-day notice APAC sent after missed installment payments
The automated email sent after an uncured default, including APAC's four numbered certifications on its letterhead
Automatic cancellation by GoAuto's computer system upon receipt of the email
The later use of a signature stamp by an APAC employee on printed documents
The plaintiffs' argument that no cancellation can occur until a signed certification exists
The statutory text's silence on signatures and the court's focus on the word 'certifying'
How the court used Louisiana intermediate-appellate decisions such as KMJ Services and Hodges
Benitez v. Elsayed and why the Fifth Circuit treated its signature discussion as non-dispositive
The court's key interpretive move: the statute speaks of the company certifying information, not a named individual signing it
Why 'strict adherence' means following the statute exactly, not judicially expanding it
The holding on this issue: Louisiana law does not require a pre-cancellation signature on the finance company's notice

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: 'Receipt' in the Digital Age — Whether GoAuto Properly Received the Cancellation Request
outline.description: This chapter addresses the plaintiffs' second major argument: that GoAuto never 'received' APAC's cancellation request before cancellation occurred. It examines the pre-2017 and post-2017 document-handling practices, the statutory significance of 'receipt,' the court's use of ordinary legal definitions, and the conclusion that electronic delivery to GoAuto's computer system constituted sufficient possession or custody under the statute. It also notes the district court's separate 'private carrier' theory and why the Fifth Circuit did not rely on it.
subtopics: Why the statutory word 'receipt' mattered to the plaintiffs' theory of ineffective cancellation
The plaintiffs' challenges to GoAuto's possession of the request before and after 2017
The pre-2017 shared filing-cabinet arrangement
The post-2017 practice of an APAC employee obtaining a GoAuto 'received' stamp and filing the printed document
The court's reliance on ordinary definitions of 'receipt' and 'receive' from Black's Law Dictionary
The standard adopted by the Fifth Circuit: possession, delivery, or custody is enough
How the APAC system communicated with a GoAuto web service to request or perform cancellation
The court's treatment of automated computer-to-computer communication as modern statutory receipt
Why no human involvement was required before the insurer could act
The holding on this issue: GoAuto's electronic intake and automatic response satisfied section 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i)
The district court's alternative 'private carrier' reasoning
Why the Fifth Circuit found that alternative theory unnecessary once email receipt was deemed sufficient

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 5: Certification, Disposition, and the Opinion's Practical Significance
outline.description: This chapter concludes the case by explaining the plaintiffs' request to certify state-law questions to the Louisiana Supreme Court, the Fifth Circuit's reluctance to certify absent compelling reasons, and the final affirmance of summary judgment for GoAuto. It also clarifies the opinion's practical importance: it approves electronic, automated compliance with Louisiana's financed-policy cancellation statute while insisting that strict adherence remains tied to statutory text rather than extra formalities.
subtopics: The plaintiffs' request to certify the statutory-interpretation issues to the Louisiana Supreme Court
The Fifth Circuit's general approach to certification and its caution against overuse
Why the absence of controlling Louisiana Supreme Court precedent did not justify certification here
How the court's statutory conclusions resolved the plaintiffs' challenge to denial of their own summary-judgment motion
The final judgment: affirmance of the district court in full
What the opinion means for insurers and premium finance companies using electronic cancellation systems
The case's narrower doctrinal lesson: strict compliance with a statute does not authorize courts to impose unstated signature or paper-delivery requirements
